title: The Cartographer of My Own Attention
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] I began, somewhat obsessively, tracking every app I opened for a month, less out of discipline than a nagging suspicion that my own account of my days had grown quietly unreliable.
Narrator: The suspicion, it turns out, was generous to myself; the actual figures were considerably more damning than anything I'd braced for.
Narrator: [carefully] I had estimated perhaps ninety minutes daily surrendered to idle scrolling, a figure I'd already considered mildly embarrassing, and the true number nearly tripled it.

Narrator: What unsettled me wasn't merely the volume but the total absence of memory attached to it, entire evenings that had simply evaporated without leaving behind a single retrievable image or thought.

Narrator: [reflective] Compare that to an hour spent reading, which I can usually reconstruct in some detail weeks later, and you begin to suspect that not all hours are created equal, however identically the clock renders them.
Narrator: Some hours accumulate, becoming part of the architecture of a person; others simply pass through, leaving no more residue than water through an open hand.

Narrator: [honestly] I don't say this as an indictment of the platforms alone, tempting as that convenient villain remains; I chose, each time, to open the application, however thoroughly its design conspired against my closing it again.
Narrator: So I've become, rather grandly, the cartographer of my own attention, mapping where it actually travels rather than where I'd like to believe it goes.

Narrator: [gently] The map is unflattering, as most honest maps of the self tend to be, but at least it's now accurate, which strikes me as the necessary precondition for revising the territory at all.

Narrator: I haven't reclaimed all those evaporated hours, and perhaps I never fully will. But I notice the vanishing now, in real time, which is a considerably more modest achievement than reform, and a considerably more honest one.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator begin tracking every app he opened for a month?
options: A nagging suspicion that his own account of his days had grown unreliable
A workplace requirement
A challenge from a friend
He wanted to sell the data
quiz.explanation: He began tracking out of a nagging suspicion that his account of his days had become unreliable.

quiz.question: How did the actual figures compare to the narrator's estimate?
options: They matched exactly
The true number nearly tripled his estimate of ninety minutes daily
The true number was lower than expected
He refused to calculate them
quiz.explanation: He had estimated ninety minutes daily, but the true figure nearly tripled that estimate.

quiz.question: What unsettled the narrator most about the scrolling time?
options: The cost of his phone plan
That his friends knew about it
The total absence of memory attached to it, with entire evenings evaporating
The battery drain on his phone
quiz.explanation: He was most unsettled by the complete absence of retrievable memory from those scrolling hours.

quiz.question: What comparison does the narrator draw with reading?
options: Reading and scrolling produce identical memories
Reading is always more enjoyable
Reading takes more time than scrolling
An hour of reading can usually be reconstructed in detail weeks later, unlike scrolling
quiz.explanation: He contrasts scrolling with reading, which he can often reconstruct in detail weeks later.

quiz.question: What does the narrator call himself after starting this tracking practice?
options: The cartographer of his own attention
A victim of technology
A digital minimalist expert
An addict beyond help
quiz.explanation: He describes himself as having become the cartographer of his own attention, mapping where it actually travels.

quiz.question: What central claim does “The Cartographer of My Own Attention” develop?
options: Convenience can quietly replace forms of deliberate connection.
Attention can be mapped without becoming fully understood.
Personalisation can infer patterns without genuine understanding.
Being reachable should remain a choice, not an obligation.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects limits of automated claims and accountable technology use.

quiz.question: Which evidence best supports the reasoning in “The Cartographer of My Own Attention”?
options: The landline’s limits shape a different kind of availability.
The algorithm’s prediction exposes how much data is collected.
Tracking reveals habits but not a complete self.
Constant availability blurs work and private boundaries.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects limits of automated claims and accountable technology use.

quiz.question: Which qualification limits the claim in “The Cartographer of My Own Attention”?
options: Nostalgia does not prove older tools were universally better.
Prediction is not consent or knowledge of a person’s values.
Connectivity does not require surrendering all privacy.
Data patterns do not justify deterministic conclusions.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects limits of automated claims and accountable technology use.

quiz.question: Which response best expresses the speaker’s stance in “The Cartographer of My Own Attention”?
options: The narrator uses the map as reflection, not verdict.
The narrator weighs what was gained and lost.
The narrator questions opaque profiling.
The speaker sets deliberate limits on findability.
quiz.explanation: The answer reflects limits of automated claims and accountable technology use.

quiz.question: What implication follows most clearly from “The Cartographer of My Own Attention”?
options: Technology choices redistribute attention and access.
Measurement should support agency rather than control.
